title: What is Low level System Design ?
summary: Low Level Design is the set of in-process decisions — classes, interfaces, ownership, and invariants — that determine whether changing code is cheap or dangerous.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **Low Level Design is how you make change cheap.** High-level design decides which services exist; LLD decides whether adding one business rule takes one hour or one week. If your classes have clear owners, narrow interfaces, and explicit invariants, the codebase stays calm under pressure. If they do not, every feature becomes surgery. That is the entire game.

Low Level Design is the detailed structure of code **inside** a service or module: what objects exist, what each one owns, what methods it exposes, how objects call each other, and what rules must never be violated. It covers classes and interfaces, composition versus inheritance, ownership and lifecycles, state transitions, concurrency control at the object level, and where validation, persistence, and external calls live. It does not cover load balancers, Kafka topics, database sharding, or regions. Those are high-level design. LLD starts where the architecture diagram stops — at the box labeled *Parking Service* or *Billing* — and answers: what is inside that box, and why is it shaped that way?

Think of it as a contract for future developers. A good LLD tells the next engineer three things without them reading every line: **where does this logic belong, what can I depend on, and what will break if I change this?** That is why interviewers test it with bounded problems like parking lot, elevator, or splitwise. They are not checking whether you can build a parking lot. They are checking whether you can draw boundaries that survive the second and third requirement — *add EV spots, add dynamic pricing, add concurrency* — without collapsing the first design. LLD is judged by extensibility, not completeness.

blocks.text: The mechanism: from requirement to code that survives change

blocks.title: LLD workflow
blocks.caption: LLD is iterative: every new rule feeds back into entities and ownership.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  REQ[Requirements] --> ENT[Entities and Value Objects]
  ENT --> REL[Relationships and Ownership]
  REL --> BEH[Behaviors and Interfaces]
  BEH --> INV[Invariants and State Rules]
  INV --> CODE[Maintainable Code]
  CODE -->|New requirement| REQ

blocks.text: The mechanism is always the same, whether on a whiteboard or in production. First you extract **nouns** that hold identity and lifecycle — `ParkingLot`, `Ticket`, `Vehicle` — and separate them from **values** that are just data — `Money`, `TimeRange`, `SpotId`. Then you assign **ownership**: who creates whom, who can mutate whom, and what is the one authoritative place for each fact. Then you place **behavior** next to the data it needs, behind narrow interfaces, so callers depend on *what* is done, not *how*. Finally you state **invariants** explicitly — *a ticket cannot exit before it enters, a spot holds at most one vehicle* — and enforce them in one place. The reason for this order is economic: ownership mistakes are ten times more expensive to fix than method-naming mistakes, so you settle ownership before you argue about method signatures. The trade-off is upfront thinking time versus later debugging time, and LLD deliberately spends the former to save the latter.

items: **Entities and value objects:** entities have identity and lifecycle (`Booking`, `Account`); values are interchangeable and immutable (`Money`, `Slot`). Mixing them creates accidental mutation and bad equality checks.

**Relationships:** association, aggregation, and composition are not academic labels — they decide who deletes whom. Use composition when the child cannot outlive the parent, and the trade-off is simpler cleanup versus less reuse.

**Interfaces and dependencies:** depend on abstractions for volatile behavior like pricing, notification, or payment. The trade-off is one extra indirection versus shotgun edits when the rule changes.

**State and invariants:** model legal transitions explicitly (`AVAILABLE -> OCCUPIED -> RESERVED`), not with scattered booleans. The trade-off is slightly more code now versus impossible-to-test `if` soup later.

**Concurrency ownership:** decide which object owns the lock or the thread-safe boundary. The trade-off is coarser locking is simpler but kills throughput; finer locking is faster but easy to deadlock.
**Boundaries:** keep I/O, persistence, and domain rules in different classes. The reason is testability — business rules should be testable without a database or a network.

blocks.caption: Every LLD choice buys something and pays for it elsewhere.
rows: Abstraction and interfaces
Open for extension without editing callers; easy mocking
Indirection, more files, harder to trace for beginners
Composition over inheritance
No fragile base-class coupling; behavior assembled at runtime
More wiring code; cannot reuse protected helpers blindly
Strict SRP / small classes
Clear owner for each change; fast code review
More classes to discover; risk of anemic objects with logic leaking into services
Defensive validation + invariants
Fail fast with a clear culprit; fewer corrupt states
Duplicate checks if placed at every layer instead of one boundary
Design patterns
Shared vocabulary for recurring problems like Strategy or Observer
Over-engineering tax when applied speculatively before the second use case appears

blocks.text: The opinionated rule is this: **do not abstract for a future you cannot name.** A `PricingStrategy` interface is justified the moment the interviewer says *flat rate now, dynamic later* or production shows two pricing rules in one `if-else` chain, because the cost of the interface is one file and the payoff is zero edits to `Checkout` when rule three arrives. It is *not* justified for a one-off calculation you merely suspect might vary, because then you pay indirection on every read and get no change-resistance in return. The same logic applies to patterns: use Observer because three subscribers already need decoupled updates, not because *something might subscribe someday*. Good LLD is stingy with flexibility — it buys it exactly where change hurts most.
How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Bad LLD rarely causes a dramatic outage. It causes a slowdown that looks like incompetence but is actually structural. The classic shape is the god service: one `BookingManager` that validates input, computes price, calls the payment gateway, writes to the database, and sends notifications. It works on launch. Six months later a *small* request — *waive fees for premium users on weekends* — touches twelve `if` branches, breaks refunds, and cannot be unit-tested without spinning up a database and a mock gateway. Engineers start copying the method instead of modifying it. Dead code piles up. Velocity drops while headcount stays flat. That divergence — same team, slower output — is the signature of LLD debt, not talent debt.

items: **God class + shotgun edit:** symptom is one file everyone fears and every stack trace passes through. Change one rule, three unrelated tests fail.
**Leaky ownership:** symptom is duplicate source of truth — spot status in both `Spot` and `Ticket`, balances in both `Wallet` and `Ledger`. They drift, and reconciliation becomes a cron job.
**Primitive obsession:** symptom is `String status`, `int type`, `Map<String, Object> payload` everywhere. Invalid states compile, so bugs surface as bad data, not compile errors.
**I/O tangled with rules:** symptom is business logic that cannot be tested without network or disk. Tests are slow, flaky, and eventually skipped.
**Inheritance for reuse:** symptom is base-class edits breaking distant subclasses. You wanted code reuse; you got invisible coupling across the hierarchy.

blocks.title: The production smell to memorize
blocks.text: If a *one-line business change* requires touching five classes, or a *one-class change* breaks five features, ownership is wrong. Do not add caching, workers, or microservices to fix it. Move the behavior to its owner, narrow the interface, and pin the invariant in one place. Scale fixes throughput; only LLD fixes change-cost.

This snippet is LLD in miniature. The commented version is not wrong because it is long — it is wrong because **pricing knowledge lives in the wrong owner**. `Checkout` should coordinate checkout, not enumerate discount rules, so every pricing change forces an edit, retest, and redeploy of checkout. The Strategy version moves the volatile part behind a narrow `apply()` contract. Why is that better? Because the direction of dependency flips: `Checkout` now depends on a stable abstraction, and new rules arrive as new classes, not as edits. The trade-off is explicit: you accept one extra interface and one extra file per rule in exchange for never reopening `Checkout` for pricing reasons. That exchange is profitable only because pricing is volatile — you would not do this for a truly stable calculation.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Clarify scope and follow-ups
items.text: Ask what will vary: types of vehicles, pricing rules, concurrency, persistence? State assumptions out loud. Interviewers score this because real LLD is designing for the second requirement, not the first.

items.title: List entities and value objects
items.text: Name 4-7 core classes, no more. Distinguish identity objects from pure data. Say why each one deserves to exist — what lifecycle or invariant does it own?

items.title: Draw relationships and ownership
items.text: Sketch a class diagram: composition vs association, multiplicities, who creates and deletes whom. Defend one ownership call explicitly and name its trade-off.

items.title: Assign behavior and contracts
items.text: Write key method signatures, not full bodies. Show inputs, outputs, and who validates what. Keep interfaces narrow so callers cannot reach into internals.

items.title: Handle the delta
items.text: Expect: add a feature, make it thread-safe, or persist it. Show extension without rewrite — new subclass or strategy, synchronized at the owning object, repository behind an interface. This is where offers are won.

items.title: Discuss testability and failure
items.text: Explain how you would unit-test rules without I/O, what invariant violation throws, and where concurrency can break. Close by stating what you would *not* build yet and why.

items: **LLD is UML diagrams.** No — diagrams are notation. LLD is ownership and dependency decisions. A neat diagram of a bad design still fails the follow-up.

**LLD is memorizing 23 patterns.** Patterns are vocabulary, not a checklist. Naming *Strategy* correctly earns nothing if you apply it where nothing varies. Interviewers penalize speculative patterns.
**SOLID means always.** Each principle has a cost. Strict Interface Segregation on a stable internal helper just fragments the code. State when you are deliberately violating a principle and why.
**More classes means better design.** Beyond 7-9 core classes for a 45-minute problem, you are signaling inability to prioritize. Group trivia, elevate volatile behavior.

**LLD and HLD are interchangeable.** Adding a queue does not fix a god class, and splitting a class does not fix a hotspot. They solve different bottlenecks — change-cost versus load — and conflating them wastes both.
**Working code is enough.** In an LLD round, code that passes but cannot absorb the stated extension is a reject. Extensibility is the test, not compilation.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Apply LLD rigor proportional to lifespan and change rate.
rows: Long-lived domain logic (billing, booking, game rules)
Full LLD
Change is guaranteed; ownership mistakes compound for years
45-minute OOD interview problem
Full LLD, simplified
The follow-up extension is the real question; boundaries matter more than bodies
Throwaway script or prototype
Minimal LLD
Lifespan is days; abstraction tax exceeds change savings
CRUD with no rules or variation
Thin LLD
Anemic model plus a repository is fine; do not invent strategies for stable reads/writes
Performance-critical inner loop
Defer clean abstractions locally
Virtual dispatch and allocation have a cost; isolate the fast path, keep the boundary clean

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Low Level Design is deciding classes, ownership, and interfaces so that the next requirement changes one place, not five — and I trade a little indirection now to avoid shotgun edits later.** Say that, then prove it with one ownership decision and one extension that needs no rewrite.
